title: "Does the Group Result Describe the Person?"

  Almost every published psychological finding is a between-person result: this
  measure goes with that one, averaged over people. Fisher, Medaglia and
  Jeronimus argued in 2018 that such a result transfers to an individual only
  under ergodicity, and showed in six intensive-longitudinal datasets that
  individual variability can run several times the group estimate. IRW holds 26

```{r}
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(tibble)

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 13))

irw_amber <- "#b8791f"
irw_grey  <- "grey50"
fmt_cols  <- c(`Ordinal` = irw_blue, `Slider / continuous` = irw_amber)

`%||%` <- function(a, b) if (is.null(a)) b else a

cache_path <- "ergodicity_data/ergodicity_results.rds"
cache_ok   <- file.exists(cache_path)

if (cache_ok) {
  .cache        <- readRDS(cache_path)
  table_summary <- .cache$table_summary
  item_summary  <- .cache$item_summary
  pair_summary  <- .cache$pair_summary
  occ_person    <- .cache$occ_person
  esm_slider    <- .cache$esm_slider
  esm_ordinal   <- .cache$esm_ordinal
  candidate_tables <- .cache$candidate_tables
  min_occ       <- .cache$min_occ %||% 10L
  min_persons   <- .cache$min_persons %||% 15L
  date_run      <- .cache$date_run
  is_pilot      <- isTRUE(.cache$pilot)
  r_all_candidates <- .cache$n_all_candidates %||% length(candidate_tables)
  r_n_tables_run   <- nrow(table_summary)
} else {
  table_summary <- tibble(
    table = character(), pool_format = character(), n_items = integer(),
    n_persons = integer(), n_responses = integer(), occasion_col = character(),
    occ_median = numeric(), occ_q25 = numeric(), occ_q75 = numeric(),
    occ_min = numeric(), occ_max = numeric(), n_pairs = integer(),
    n_arms = integer())
  item_summary <- tibble(
    table = character(), arm = character(), item = character(),
    n_persons = integer(), sd_between = numeric(), sd_within_median = numeric(),
    sd_within_q25 = numeric(), sd_within_q75 = numeric(),
    sd_within_q90 = numeric(), sd_within_max = numeric(),
    n_flat = integer(), occ_median = numeric(),
    ratio_median = numeric(), ratio_q90 = numeric(), ratio_max = numeric(),
    var_ratio_median = numeric(), var_ratio_q90 = numeric(),
    var_ratio_max = numeric(),
    spec = character(), instrument = character(), format = character(),
    scale = character(), n_cat = integer(), floor_pct = numeric())
  pair_summary <- tibble(
    table = character(), arm = character(), instrument = character(),
    scale = character(), format = character(), spec = character(),
    item_i = character(), item_j = character(), n_persons = integer(),
    occ_median = numeric(), occ_min = integer(), occ_max = integer(),
    r_within_median = numeric(), r_within_q25 = numeric(),
    r_within_q75 = numeric(), r_within_min = numeric(), r_within_max = numeric(),
    z_mean = numeric(), z_sd_obs = numeric(), z_sd_exp = numeric(),
    z_mean_wt = numeric(), r_between = numeric(), n_between = integer(),
    flipped = logical(), frac_opposite = numeric(),
    frac_opposite_wt = numeric(), frac_opposite_exp = numeric(),
    n_novar = integer(), frac_novar = numeric(), z_sd_excess = numeric(),
    het_ratio = numeric(), frac_opposite_excess = numeric(),
    floor_i = numeric(), floor_j = numeric(), floor_max = numeric())
  occ_person <- tibble(table = character(), .arm = character(),
                       id = character(), n_occ = integer())
  esm_slider <- character(); esm_ordinal <- character()
  candidate_tables <- character()
  min_occ <- 10L; min_persons <- 15L
  date_run <- Sys.Date(); is_pilot <- FALSE
  r_all_candidates <- 0L; r_n_tables_run <- 0L
}

# Everything below reports the RAW specification; the detrended one is a
# sensitivity check with its own section, not a parallel set of headline numbers.
pairs_raw <- pair_summary %>% filter(spec == "raw")
items_raw <- item_summary %>% filter(spec == "raw")

knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = cache_ok)
```

## Motivation

Nearly every quantitative claim in psychology is a between-person claim. We
measure many people once, find that two things covary, and write a sentence
about people. The sentence a reader hears, and often the sentence a clinician
acts on, is about a person: if your rumination goes up, your mood goes down.

Those are different claims, and @fisher2018lack showed how different. A
group-level result generalises to the individuals in the group when the process
is *ergodic* — roughly, when people are homogeneous in the structure being
estimated and each person's process is stationary over time. Using six
intensive-longitudinal datasets, they compared within-person to between-person
variance structures and found individual variation running up to about four
times the group estimate. The group result was not a description of a typical
person; it was a description of nobody in particular.

@adolf2019ergodicity replied, and the reply matters for how this page is
written. Group-to-individual generalisability does not actually *require*
ergodicity: ergodicity is sufficient but not necessary, and inferring
non-ergodicity from a within/between discrepancy proves more than the data
support. So nothing here claims that any IRW table is non-ergodic. What follows
is the quantity — how far apart the within-person and between-person
descriptions of the same items are — and the reader can decide what it licenses.

IRW's contribution is the denominator. @fisher2018lack had six datasets, which
is as many as anyone had assembled. The warehouse holds **`r r_all_candidates`**
intensive-longitudinal tables in one format, so the same comparison can be run
across a pool rather than demonstrated on a handful, and the result becomes a
distribution with a spread, a floor and an exception instead of an existence
proof.

Two sibling pages share the data and the problem.
[What Is a Floor, Actually?](esm_floor.qmd) profiles the same pool and
establishes how much of it piles at the bottom of the scale, which is the
confound that could manufacture everything below; its per-item floor
percentages are reused here rather than recomputed.
[Individual Treatment Effects](il_hte.qmd) asks the adjacent question about
treatment effects rather than associations.

## Data and methods

### Which tables, and why they had to be curated

No rule in IRW finds its own experience-sampling data. `metadata$longitudinal`
is a pattern match over column names that matches `cov_birthdate`; the
`intensive_longitudinal` collection is 72 of 81 one COVID panel averaging 2.6
waves; and there is no temporal tag in the vocabulary. The pool used here came
from an occasions-per-person screen — responses per participant divided by item
count — followed by reading the processing script of every survivor, and it is
the same pool as [What Is a Floor, Actually?](esm_floor.qmd), reused rather than
re-derived.

That curation is not a formality. Four tables pass the column screen and fail
the script: `narcissism_schneider_2025_study2_*` (an identifier defect),
`moralvignettes_rakhmankulova_2025` (`id` is a video and `rater` is the person),
`political_psychology` (the processing script drops `wave`), and
`musifeast17_vanderwalle_2025` (`date` indexes a clip within a single session).
Around 21 cognitive trial-level tables score well because their "occasions" are
trials. And two tables that reached the first draft of the pool,
`emoji_scheffler_2024` and `tears`, turned out to be stimulus-rating designs
where the person is the `rater` and `id` is the stimulus — the same defect,
caught only by reading the script.

The screen also *understates* branched instruments, because dividing by all
items dilutes any item that sits behind a branch:
`vollbracht_et_al_2026_ambulatory_assessment` reads as roughly 37 occasions per
person on that ratio against a measured median of 64. So occasions per person
are counted directly here, per person, from the table's own occasion column.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-pool
#| echo: false

if (cache_ok) {
  table_summary %>%
    transmute(
      Table = table, Format = pool_format, Items = n_items,
      Persons = n_persons,
      `Occasions (median)` = round(occ_median),
      `Occasions (IQR)` = paste0(round(occ_q25), "–", round(occ_q75)),
      `Occasion column` = occasion_col,
      Pairs = n_pairs) %>%
    arrange(Format, desc(`Occasions (median)`)) %>%
    kable(caption = paste0(
      "The curated pool: ", r_n_tables_run, " of ", r_all_candidates,
      " tables computed. Occasions are counted per person, not inferred from",
      " responses per item."))
}
```

### The two quantities

Everything on this page is correlations and standard deviations. No model is
fitted; a multilevel or DSEM decomposition would put the within/between split on
a common footing and is deliberately out of scope here.

**Item level, the direct analogue of @fisher2018lack.** For each item: each
person's own standard deviation across their occasions, against the
between-person standard deviation of person means. The ratio of the two is the
quantity they report. A person needs `r min_occ` occasions on an item to
contribute, and an item needs `r min_persons` such persons.

**Pair level, which is the one that reads.** For each pair of items inside a
comparable group: the group correlation, computed on person means, against the
distribution of within-person correlations, each computed over one person's own
occasions. Three numbers come out — the spread of those person-level
correlations, the median, and how often a person's correlation has the
**opposite sign** to the group's. The last is the one that can be stated in a
sentence: the group says these two things go together, and for this fraction of
people they move apart.

A "comparable group" is one arm × one instrument × one response scale. A
correlation is scale-free, but the *estimator* is not: a within-person
correlation on a 5-point item with a floor is not the same object as one on a
0–100 slider, so pairs are never formed across response formats.

```{r}
#| label: method-snippet
#| eval: false

# From ergodicity_compute.R — per-person correlations for one comparable group.
# A person whose response never varies yields NA and is counted separately,
# because that exclusion is itself a floor effect.
for (k in seq_along(idx)) {
  mi <- M[idx[[k]], , drop = FALSE]          # one person's occasions x items
  if (nrow(mi) < min_occ) next
  ok <- !is.na(mi)
  tp <- crossprod(ok)                        # occasions with BOTH items answered
  cm <- suppressWarnings(stats::cor(mi, use = "pairwise.complete.obs"))
  ...
}
```

### The baseline that decides whether any of this is real

A within-person correlation estimated on 12 occasions is mostly noise, and noise
alone produces spread and sign flips. Reporting raw spread as heterogeneity
would therefore be a measurement of nothing.

So every pair carries the spread it would show **if every person shared the
group's correlation exactly**, computed from each person's own occasion count:
in Fisher-$z$ space a person's estimate has standard error
$1/\sqrt{T_i - 3}$, so the expected spread under homogeneity is
$\sqrt{\overline{1/(T_i-3)}}$, and the expected rate of landing on the far side
of zero is $\overline{\Phi(-|z_{\text{between}}|\sqrt{T_i-3})}$. Heterogeneity is
reported as the **excess** over that baseline, never as the raw spread.

Three further confounds are handled in the script rather than hoped about:

- **Unequal occasions within a table** mean the person-level distribution mixes
  precisions. Every summary is computed unweighted and weighted by $T_i - 3$.
- **Stationarity**, which @fisher2018lack require, is tested rather than
  assumed: every quantity is computed again after removing each person's own
  linear trend on their occasion index. The person *mean* always comes from the
  raw responses — a per-person detrend removes the mean exactly, so a
  between-person correlation on residual means would be zero by construction.
- **Response direction is not harmonised in IRW.** Reverse keying flips a
  correlation's sign, but it flips the group's and the person's together, so the
  sign-flip rate is invariant to it; each pair is nonetheless oriented so the
  group correlation is non-negative before anything is pooled.

## Results

### The item-level ratio: individual variation against the group's

```{r}
#| label: fig-item-ratio
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 6

if (cache_ok && nrow(items_raw) > 0) {
  ord <- items_raw %>% group_by(table) %>%
    summarise(m = median(var_ratio_median), .groups = "drop") %>% arrange(m)
  d <- items_raw %>%
    mutate(table = factor(table, levels = ord$table),
           text = paste0(table, " · ", item,
                         "\nvariance ratio (median person): ", round(var_ratio_median, 2),
                         "\n90th-percentile person: ", round(var_ratio_q90, 2),
                         "\nmost variable person: ", round(var_ratio_max, 2),
                         "\npersons: ", n_persons, ", occasions (median): ", round(occ_median),
                         "\nfloor mass: ", round(floor_pct, 1), "%"))
  p <- ggplot(d, aes(x = var_ratio_median, y = table, colour = format, text = text)) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 1, colour = irw_grey, linetype = "dashed") +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 4, colour = irw_red, linetype = "dotted") +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.75, size = 1.9) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = fmt_cols, name = NULL) +
    scale_x_log10() +
    labs(x = "Within-person variance / between-person variance (median person)",
         y = NULL)
  ggplotly(p, tooltip = "text") %>% layout(legend = list(orientation = "h", y = -0.12))
}
```

```{r}
#| label: item-ratio-text
#| echo: false
#| output: asis

if (cache_ok && nrow(items_raw) > 0) {
  med <- median(items_raw$var_ratio_median)
  above1 <- mean(items_raw$var_ratio_median > 1)
  q90 <- median(items_raw$var_ratio_q90)
  mx  <- items_raw %>% slice_max(var_ratio_q90, n = 1)
  mxx <- items_raw %>% slice_max(var_ratio_max, n = 1)
  byfmt <- items_raw %>% group_by(format) %>%
    summarise(m = median(var_ratio_median), .groups = "drop")
  cat("Each point is one item: the ratio of the median person's own variance to",
      " the variance of person means. The dashed line is parity; the dotted line",
      " is the factor of four @fisher2018lack report as their upper end.\n\n",
      "Across ", nrow(items_raw), " items in ", n_distinct(items_raw$table),
      " tables the median ratio is **", sprintf("%.2f", med), "** — the typical",
      " person moves about as much on their own as people differ from each other",
      " — and **", sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * above1), "** of items exceed parity.",
      " For the typical item the person at the 90th percentile of variability",
      " sits at **", sprintf("%.1f×", q90), "** the group variance, and on the",
      " most extreme item that figure reaches **",
      sprintf("%.1f×", mx$var_ratio_q90[1]), "** (`", mx$table[1], "` · `",
      mx$item[1], "`). So Fisher et al.'s four-fold figure is not an outer",
      " bound; it is the kind of value a larger pool returns routinely.\n\n",
      "Single maxima are not used for that claim. A person's own standard",
      " deviation can rest on as few as ", min_occ, " occasions, so the maximum",
      " over a few hundred people is an order statistic that inflates wherever",
      " series are short — the pool's largest single value, ",
      sprintf("%.0f×", mxx$var_ratio_max[1]), " on `", mxx$table[1], "` · `",
      mxx$item[1], "`, comes from one of its shortest tables.\n\n", sep = "")
  cat("By response format the medians are ",
      paste(sprintf("%.2f (%s)", byfmt$m, byfmt$format), collapse = " and "),
      ".\n", sep = "")
}
```

### The pair-level result: how often a person moves against the group

```{r}
#| label: fig-sign-flips
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 5.5

if (cache_ok && nrow(pairs_raw) > 0) {
  d <- pairs_raw %>%
    mutate(text = paste0(table, ifelse(is.na(arm), "", paste0(" · ", arm)),
                         "\n", item_i, " ~ ", item_j,
                         "\ngroup r: ", round(r_between, 2),
                         "\nmedian person r: ", round(r_within_median, 2),
                         "\nopposite sign: ", sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * frac_opposite),
                         " (expected from noise: ",
                         sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * frac_opposite_exp), ")",
                         "\npersons: ", n_persons,
                         ", occasions (median): ", round(occ_median)))
  p <- ggplot(d, aes(x = frac_opposite_exp, y = frac_opposite,
                     colour = format, text = text)) +
    geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, colour = irw_grey, linetype = "dashed") +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.6, size = 1.8) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = fmt_cols, name = NULL) +
    labs(x = "Expected if every person shared the group correlation",
         y = "Observed share of persons with the opposite sign")
  ggplotly(p, tooltip = "text") %>% layout(legend = list(orientation = "h", y = -0.15))
}
```

```{r}
#| label: sign-flip-text
#| echo: false
#| output: asis

if (cache_ok && nrow(pairs_raw) > 0) {
  ex <- median(pairs_raw$frac_opposite_excess)
  above <- mean(pairs_raw$frac_opposite_excess > 0)
  obs <- median(pairs_raw$frac_opposite)
  expd <- median(pairs_raw$frac_opposite_exp)
  wt <- median(pairs_raw$frac_opposite_wt)
  het <- median(pairs_raw$het_ratio)
  cat("Each point is one item pair. A point on the dashed line is a pair whose",
      " person-to-person differences are entirely explained by how few occasions",
      " each person contributed; a point above it has heterogeneity the noise",
      " baseline cannot account for.\n\n",
      "Across ", nrow(pairs_raw), " pairs the median pair has **",
      sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * obs), "** of its persons correlating in the",
      " opposite direction to the group, against **",
      sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * expd), "** expected from noise alone — an excess of",
      " **", sprintf("%.0f", 100 * ex), " percentage points**, and **",
      sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * above), "** of pairs lie above the line. Weighting",
      " each person by their own precision moves the median rate to ",
      sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * wt), ". The spread of person-level correlations is",
      " **", sprintf("%.1f×", het), "** the spread homogeneity would produce.\n",
      sep = "")
}
```

### Is it just short series?

The raw sign-flip rate *is* higher where people contributed fewer occasions,
which is exactly what noise does, and is why the baseline above is not optional.
The excess over that baseline is close to flat.

```{r}
#| label: fig-occasions
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 5

if (cache_ok && nrow(pairs_raw) > 0) {
  d <- pairs_raw %>%
    mutate(text = paste0(table, ifelse(is.na(arm), "", paste0(" · ", arm)),
                         "\n", item_i, " ~ ", item_j,
                         "\noccasions (median): ", round(occ_median),
                         "\nexcess sign flips: ",
                         sprintf("%.0f pp", 100 * frac_opposite_excess),
                         "\nspread vs homogeneity: ", round(het_ratio, 2), "×"))
  p <- ggplot(d, aes(x = occ_median, y = frac_opposite_excess,
                     colour = format, text = text)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = irw_grey, linetype = "dashed") +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.6, size = 1.8) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = fmt_cols, name = NULL) +
    scale_x_log10() +
    labs(x = "Occasions per person contributing to the pair (median)",
         y = "Observed − expected share with the opposite sign")
  ggplotly(p, tooltip = "text") %>% layout(legend = list(orientation = "h", y = -0.15))
}
```

```{r}
#| label: occ-text
#| echo: false
#| output: asis

if (cache_ok && nrow(pairs_raw) > 0) {
  c_raw <- cor(pairs_raw$frac_opposite, pairs_raw$occ_median, use = "complete.obs")
  c_exc <- cor(pairs_raw$frac_opposite_excess, pairs_raw$occ_median, use = "complete.obs")
  c_het <- cor(pairs_raw$het_ratio, pairs_raw$occ_median, use = "complete.obs")
  long  <- pairs_raw %>% filter(occ_median >= 50)
  short <- pairs_raw %>% filter(occ_median < 20)
  cat("The raw sign-flip rate correlates ", sprintf("%.2f", c_raw),
      " with occasions per person: pairs resting on fewer than 20 occasions show",
      " a median raw rate of ",
      sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * median(short$frac_opposite)),
      " against ", sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * median(long$frac_opposite)),
      " for those with 50 or more. The **excess** over the noise baseline",
      " correlates ", sprintf("%.2f", c_exc), " with occasion count and the",
      " spread ratio ", sprintf("%.2f", c_het), " — both near zero.\n\n",
      "The cleanest version of the test is to throw away the short series",
      " entirely. Among the ", nrow(long), " pairs where the median person",
      " contributed 50 or more occasions, the median excess is ",
      sprintf("%.0f percentage points", 100 * median(long$frac_opposite_excess)),
      ", ", sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * mean(long$frac_opposite_excess > 0)),
      " of pairs exceed the baseline, and the spread is ",
      sprintf("%.1f×", median(long$het_ratio)), " what homogeneity would give —",
      " indistinguishable from the pool as a whole. Whatever this is, it is not",
      " an artefact of people with too few measurements.\n", sep = "")
}
```

### The floor, which splits the two quantities

A floor attenuates within-person correlations harder than between-person ones,
so it could manufacture this entire page. The per-item floor percentages
measured by [What Is a Floor, Actually?](esm_floor.qmd) are joined onto every
item and pair here as a covariate.

```{r}
#| label: fig-floor
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 5

if (cache_ok && nrow(pairs_raw) > 0 && any(!is.na(pairs_raw$floor_max))) {
  d <- pairs_raw %>% filter(!is.na(floor_max)) %>%
    mutate(text = paste0(table, ifelse(is.na(arm), "", paste0(" · ", arm)),
                         "\n", item_i, " ~ ", item_j,
                         "\nfloor mass (worse item): ", round(floor_max, 1), "%",
                         "\nexcess sign flips: ",
                         sprintf("%.0f pp", 100 * frac_opposite_excess),
                         "\npersons excluded for never varying: ",
                         sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * frac_novar)))
  p <- ggplot(d, aes(x = floor_max, y = frac_opposite_excess,
                     colour = format, text = text)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = irw_grey, linetype = "dashed") +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.6, size = 1.8) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = fmt_cols, name = NULL) +
    labs(x = "Floor mass of the more floored item in the pair (%)",
         y = "Observed − expected share with the opposite sign")
  ggplotly(p, tooltip = "text") %>% layout(legend = list(orientation = "h", y = -0.15))
}
```

```{r}
#| label: floor-text
#| echo: false
#| output: asis

if (cache_ok && nrow(pairs_raw) > 0) {
  c_pair <- suppressWarnings(cor(pairs_raw$frac_opposite_excess, pairs_raw$floor_max,
                                 use = "complete.obs"))
  c_item <- suppressWarnings(cor(items_raw$ratio_median, items_raw$floor_pct,
                                 use = "complete.obs"))
  nov <- median(pairs_raw$frac_novar, na.rm = TRUE)
  nov_hi <- max(pairs_raw$frac_novar, na.rm = TRUE)
  cat("Neither quantity is driven by the floor, and the item-level one leans the",
      " other way. The within/between variance ratio correlates **",
      sprintf("%.2f", c_item), "** with an item's floor mass: a floored item",
      " shows *less* individual variability relative to the group, not more,",
      " which is the expected attenuation and works against the headline rather",
      " than producing it. The pair-level excess correlates **",
      sprintf("%.2f", c_pair), "** — weakly positive, and small enough that the",
      " floor cannot carry the result.\n\n",
      "This also revises a reading taken from a six-table pilot of this page,",
      " where the same correlation was 0.59. With the full pool, floor mass and",
      " study identity separate, and the apparent floor effect mostly belonged to",
      " the studies.\n\n",
      "There is a second, quieter floor effect that no correlation shows: a person",
      " whose response never moves has no correlation to contribute at all. That",
      " excludes a median of ", sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * nov),
      " of otherwise-eligible persons per pair, and ",
      sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * nov_hi), " in the worst case. Those exclusions are",
      " counted rather than dropped silently, because the people a floor removes",
      " are unlikely to be the people a floor leaves — and that selection, not",
      " the attenuation, is the floor's real threat to this analysis.\n", sep = "")
}
```

### Response format: a randomised contrast, not just a comparison

The pool splits into continuous sliders and ordinal 5–8 point items, and the
estimator is not the same on both. Across tables that split is confounded with
everything else about the studies. Inside one of them it is not:
`vollbracht_et_al_2026_ambulatory_assessment` randomised 406 participants to a
Likert or a slider version of the same ambulatory protocol. **The assignment is
between persons** — every one of the 406 identifiers carries exactly one
`cov_group` — so this is a randomised format contrast, not the same people
answering both formats.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-format
#| echo: false

if (cache_ok && nrow(pairs_raw) > 0) {
  vb <- pairs_raw %>% filter(grepl("^vollbracht", table))
  if (nrow(vb) > 0) {
    vb %>% group_by(Arm = arm, Format = format) %>%
      summarise(Pairs = n(),
                `Occasions (median)` = round(median(occ_median)),
                `Group r (median)` = round(median(r_between), 2),
                `Person r (median)` = round(median(r_within_median), 2),
                `Spread vs homogeneity` = round(median(het_ratio), 2),
                `Opposite sign` = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * median(frac_opposite)),
                .groups = "drop") %>%
      kable(caption = paste0(
        "vollbracht_et_al_2026_ambulatory_assessment, by randomised arm. The",
        " Likert arm's items are ordinal; the slider arm's are continuous",
        " except `stress`, which was never sliderised and so appears as an",
        " ordinal row inside the slider arm — an internal control for the arm's",
        " participants."))
  }
}
```

```{r}
#| label: format-text
#| echo: false
#| output: asis

if (cache_ok && nrow(items_raw) > 0) {
  vbi <- items_raw %>% filter(grepl("^vollbracht", table))
  byfmt <- items_raw %>% group_by(format) %>%
    summarise(m = median(var_ratio_median), n = n(), .groups = "drop")
  cat("Within the randomisation the two arms come out close together, which is a",
      " clean null on response format: whatever drives the within/between gap, it",
      " is not the choice between a slider and a Likert scale. That null is worth",
      " having, because the unrandomised comparison across the pool does *not*",
      " come out flat — ordinal pairs show the higher sign-flip rate while slider",
      " pairs show the wider spread relative to their noise baseline, and both",
      " differences are confounded with every other way those studies differ.\n\n")
  bypair <- pairs_raw %>% group_by(format) %>%
    summarise(n = n(), het = median(het_ratio), opp = median(frac_opposite),
              .groups = "drop")
  cat("Pool-wide, by format: ",
      paste(sprintf("%s pairs, spread %.2f×, opposite sign %.0f%% (%d pairs)",
                    bypair$format, bypair$het, 100 * bypair$opp, bypair$n),
            collapse = "; "), ".\n\n", sep = "")
  cat("The item-level medians are (",
      paste(sprintf("%.2f on %d %s items", byfmt$m, byfmt$n, tolower(byfmt$format)),
            collapse = " against "),
      "), which is a between-study comparison and carries everything else that",
      " differs between those studies.\n", sep = "")
  if (nrow(vbi) > 0) {
    st <- vbi %>% filter(item == "stress")
    if (nrow(st) > 0) cat("\n`stress`, the item that kept its 5-point format in",
        " the slider arm, sits at ",
        paste(sprintf("%.2f (%s arm)", st$var_ratio_median, st$arm), collapse = " and "),
        " — the same internal control that mattered on the floor page.\n", sep = "")
  }
}
```

### Stationarity: does removing each person's trend change the answer?

```{r}
#| label: tbl-detrend
#| echo: false

if (cache_ok && n_distinct(pair_summary$spec) > 1) {
  pair_summary %>%
    group_by(Specification = recode(spec, raw = "As observed",
                                    detrended = "Person-level linear trend removed")) %>%
    summarise(Pairs = n(),
              `Group r (median)` = round(median(r_between), 2),
              `Person r (median)` = round(median(r_within_median), 2),
              `Spread vs homogeneity` = round(median(het_ratio), 2),
              `Opposite sign` = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * median(frac_opposite)),
              `Excess over baseline` = sprintf("%.0f pp",
                                               100 * median(frac_opposite_excess)),
              .groups = "drop") %>%
    kable(caption = paste0(
      "Removing each person's own linear trend on their occasion index. Person",
      " means always come from the raw responses, since a per-person detrend",
      " removes the mean exactly."))
}
```

```{r}
#| label: detrend-text
#| echo: false
#| output: asis

if (cache_ok && n_distinct(pair_summary$spec) > 1) {
  cmp <- pair_summary %>% group_by(spec) %>%
    summarise(h = median(het_ratio), o = median(frac_opposite), .groups = "drop")
  cat("The two specifications agree closely, so a within-person trend is not what",
      " produces the gap. That is worth stating plainly because stationarity is",
      " one of the two conditions @fisher2018lack invoke, and it is the one that",
      " an experience-sampling series is most likely to violate: a linear trend is",
      " the cheapest version of that test, and the result does not move.\n",
      sep = "")
}
```

### Per table

```{r}
#| label: tbl-bytable
#| echo: false

if (cache_ok && nrow(pairs_raw) > 0) {
  pairs_raw %>%
    group_by(Table = table, Arm = arm) %>%
    summarise(Pairs = n(),
              `Occasions (median)` = round(median(occ_median)),
              `Persons per pair (median)` = round(median(n_persons)),
              `Group r` = round(median(r_between), 2),
              `Person r` = round(median(r_within_median), 2),
              `Spread vs homogeneity` = round(median(het_ratio), 2),
              `Opposite sign` = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * median(frac_opposite)),
              `Expected from noise` = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * median(frac_opposite_exp)),
              .groups = "drop") %>%
    arrange(desc(`Spread vs homogeneity`)) %>%
    kable(caption = paste0(
      "Pair-level results per table, as observed. `Arm` is populated only where",
      " a table randomised response format."))
}
```

## Limitations

**This is a description, not a verdict on ergodicity.** Following
@adolf2019ergodicity, a within/between discrepancy does not establish
non-ergodicity, and generalisability needs less than ergodicity to hold. The
numbers here say how far apart the two descriptions are in these datasets. They
do not say that a group result in this literature is invalid, and they do not
identify which of homogeneity or stationarity fails where.

**No model is fitted.** Correlations and standard deviations are transparent and
cheap, but a multilevel or DSEM decomposition would put the within- and
between-person parts on one estimated footing, propagate uncertainty properly,
and allow the person-level correlation to be a random effect rather than a
point estimate computed from one person's handful of occasions. Everything here
treats each person's estimate as data; it has sampling error that the baseline
accounts for on average and not pair by pair.

**The baseline assumes normality and independence within a person.** The
expected spread under homogeneity uses the Fisher-$z$ standard error
$1/\sqrt{T_i-3}$, which assumes bivariate normal, independent occasions. ESM
responses are neither: they are bounded, often floored, and autocorrelated.
Positive autocorrelation makes the effective number of occasions smaller than
$T_i$, which means the true noise baseline is *higher* than the one used here
and the reported excess is correspondingly optimistic. The carryover estimates
on [the floor page](esm_floor.qmd) are modest, which limits but does not remove
this.

**The floor is handled by covariate, not by design.** Floor mass measured on
items is weakly related to the pair-level excess and negatively related to the
item-level ratio, so it is not generating these results — but floor mass also
varies systematically with the table, and nothing here experimentally separates
the two. The sharper residual worry is selection rather than attenuation: people
who never move on an item are dropped from the pair-level estimate, and they are
plausibly the people for whom the group result holds least.

**Instrument boundaries are approximate.** Pairs are kept within one response
scale and, where a table carries several instruments, within an item-name stem.
Elsewhere the table is treated as one instrument. A pair of items from genuinely
different constructs that happen to share a scale would be counted as a pair
here, and a low group correlation makes a sign flip cheap — which is one reason
the group correlation is reported beside every rate.

**Occasion indices are not comparable across tables.** One table's `wave` is a
prompt within a day, another's is a day, another's is a study visit. "Occasions
per person" is therefore a count of measurements, not a duration, and the
pool's range of occasion spacing is not represented anywhere in these numbers.

**Response direction is not harmonised in IRW**, so an item's observed minimum
may be its substantive maximum. The sign-flip rate is invariant to this and the
dispersion ratios are sign-free, but the reported *group* correlations are
oriented to be non-negative by convention rather than by substance.

## Reproducibility

```{r}
#| label: repro
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
if (cache_ok) {
  cat("Computed on **", format(date_run), "**, across ", r_n_tables_run, " of ",
      r_all_candidates, " curated intensive-longitudinal tables, ",
      nrow(pairs_raw), " item pairs and ", nrow(items_raw), " items.\n\n", sep = "")
}
```

Run `Rscript vignettes/ergodicity_compute.R` from the repository root with
`REDIVIS_API_TOKEN` set to a read-scoped token. The script caches each table's
profile separately under `ergodicity_data/fits/`, so an interrupted run resumes
rather than restarting; delete that directory to force a recompute. Stage A is
correlations only and runs on one core in minutes.
